items.title: The Luddites were skilled workers protecting trade standards

options.text: Anti-technology mystics who rejected all machinery
Skilled textile workers — stocking knitters, croppers, weavers — who smashed specific machines being used to produce low-quality goods by unapprenticed labour, often after pay cuts and food shortages

items.reveal:
The Luddites took their name from the mythical Ned Ludd. Their grievances were specific: wide stocking frames produced cut-up goods sold as stockings; gig-mills and shearing frames replaced cropping; manufacturers were ignoring the Statute of Artificers (1563) requiring seven-year apprenticeships.

The Frame-Breaking Act (1812) made machine-breaking a capital offence — Byron made his maiden speech in the Lords opposing it. 17 Luddites were hanged at York in January 1813. The historian E. P. Thompson's 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963) rehabilitated them as political actors.
items.why: 'Luddite' as an insult against anyone who dislikes new technology obscures the actual movement. They were skilled tradesmen defending wages and standards against unregulated mechanisation — not opponents of machinery in principle.

items.title: Prohibition created modern organised crime in America
items.claim: What did Prohibition (1920-1933) actually do to alcohol consumption and crime?

options.text: Consumption fell initially but rose again; it transferred a major industry to organised criminals (Al Capone, Lucky Luciano), corrupted police and politicians, and was repealed by the 21st Amendment in December 1933
It was repealed within a year as a failure
It applied only to spirits, not beer or wine

items.reveal:
The 18th Amendment (ratified January 1919) and Volstead Act (October 1919) banned the manufacture, sale and transport of 'intoxicating liquors'. Domestic consumption was not banned; medicinal whiskey, sacramental wine and home cider remained legal.

Al Capone's Chicago Outfit reportedly grossed $100 million a year by 1927. The St Valentine's Day Massacre (14 February 1929) shocked the public. Federal income from alcohol taxes had been about 30% of federal revenue before Prohibition — its loss became politically painful during the Depression.

The 21st Amendment (December 1933) is the only constitutional amendment to repeal another.
items.why: Banning a popular consumption good creates the conditions for an illegal industry. The lesson — visible in 20th-century drug policy and elsewhere — was already clear in 1933 but is endlessly relearned.

items.title: Magna Carta was annulled within ten weeks
items.claim: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. What happened next?

options.text: It immediately became the basis of English liberty and was respected by the crown
John wrote to Pope Innocent III, who annulled it as 'shameful and demeaning' on 24 August 1215 — civil war resumed
John was forced to confirm it in Parliament the following year
It was burned by the barons after John refused to enforce it

items.reveal:
Pope Innocent III's bull of 24 August 1215 declared Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever', calling it extorted by force. The First Barons' War followed; the barons invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne.

John died of dysentery in October 1216. The charter was reissued by the regents of his nine-year-old son Henry III to win support — that is the version that took root. The 1297 reissue under Edward I is the one on the statute roll.
items.why: Magna Carta as 'the foundation of liberty' is a 17th-century invention (Coke). In 1215 it was a peace treaty between a desperate king and rebellious barons — and it failed within weeks.
